meta.title: cajulang · Simple code. Native executables.
meta.description: Caju is a simple, statically typed language that compiles straight to x86-64 machine code, producing native executables for Linux and Windows, and to WebAssembly.

title: Simple code.
Native executables.
home.lead: Caju is a simple, statically typed language that compiles straight to x86-64 machine code, producing native executables for Linux and Windows, and to WebAssembly. The compiler is written in Caju and compiles itself, and it ships with a test runner and a package manager.
home.featuresTitle: Simple to write, native to run
home.featuresLead: A lean syntax with optional types. The compiler produces a small static binary, with no runtime to install.

features.title: Native compilation
features.body: Caju compiles straight to x86-64 machine code, with no virtual machine. A hello world becomes a 52 KB static executable.

features.title: Linux, Windows and WebAssembly
features.body: Produces ELF for Linux and PE for Windows: from Linux itself, `caju build --target windows` builds an `.exe`. `--target wasm` builds a WebAssembly module that runs in Node or in the browser, like the playground.

features.title: Written in Caju
features.body: The compiler and runtime are written in the language itself. The compiler compiles itself, and the output is byte-for-byte identical.

features.title: A complete language
features.body: Structs, methods, interfaces, pointers, slices, maps, closures, defer, panic and recover, and errors as values.

features.title: Optional types
features.body: Annotate types when you want to: with them, the compiler catches errors before the program runs. Without them, types are inferred.

features.title: Standard library
features.body: strings, strconv, math, bytes, os, fs, path, net, http, json, toml, crypto, hash, hex, base64, cli and testing.

features.title: Built-in testing
features.body: `caju test` runs your `_test.caju` files with describe, it and expect, with nothing to install.

features.title: Package manager
features.body: Packages are GitHub repositories. `caju pkg` picks the versions and pins everything in a `caju.lock` with hashes.

home.codeLead: Two short programs, with the output they print. There are more on the examples page.
home.perfTitle: Side by side with Go, Rust and Python
home.perfLead: The same algorithms, with the same order of operations, in each language. Caju beats or ties Go on every challenge, stays close to Rust and is far ahead of Python.
home.sizeLead: The same program (fib), compiled in each language.
home.perfNote: Measured in November 2026 on an AMD Ryzen 7 5700G: best of up to 3 runs, including process startup. Caju 0.3.0, Go 1.27.3, Rust 1.99.1 (opt-level=3), Python 3.12.3.
home.perfLink: Full programs and results in bench/compare
home.httpTitle: HTTP server: Caju + web against Go
home.httpLead: The same JSON API written with **web**, the Caju web framework, with Gin, and with Go's standard `net/http`. On the same CPUs, Caju serves 1.5 to 2.2 times as many requests per second.
home.httpNote: Requests per second with keep-alive (higher is better). The server is pinned to its CPUs and the load generator runs on the others; Ryzen 7 5700G, WSL2. `GET /users` returns a list of 50 structs; `POST /users` reads JSON into a struct.
home.httpResults: Method and all rounds in bench/http
home.pkgLead: caju pkg ships with the language. There is no central server: a package is a GitHub repository with a caju.toml, and its name is what you import.

spec.title: Language specification
spec.lead: How Caju works: syntax, types, statements, functions, errors and modules. The examples were compiled with version {version} and show the actual output.

blocks.p: Caju is a compiled, statically typed programming language with type inference. The compiler generates x86-64 machine code: ELF executables for Linux and PE for Windows. It also generates WebAssembly modules, which run in Node and in the browser. The compiler and runtime are written in Caju itself.
The language comes with everything you need to work: a compiler, a test runner (`caju test`) and a package manager (`caju pkg`), all in a single `caju` command.
A program is one or more `.caju` files. Top-level statements run in order, from top to bottom: there is no need to declare a `main` function.
**Comments.** Start with `#` or `//` and run to the end of the line.
**Statement terminators.** A line break or a `;` ends a statement. An expression does not continue onto the next line after an operator: split it into variables.
**Identifiers.** Letters (including accented Latin letters such as `é` and `ç`), digits and `_`, not starting with a digit.
**Keywords.** These cannot be used as names:
**Literals.**

head: Type
Examples
Notes
rows: The character's code, as an integer

blocks.p: Types are optional in declarations: without an annotation, the compiler infers them. With an annotation, a value of another type is a compile error.

head: Type
Description
rows: UTF-8 text. `s[i]` is a `uint8` and `len(s)` counts bytes
Any value. Use a type assertion or type switch to recover the type

blocks.p: **Aliases.** `byte` = `uint8`, `rune` = `int32`, `string` = `str` and `float64` = `num`.

head: Composite type
Form
Behavior
rows: A window over an array; grows with `append`
Key and value; keys of basic types

blocks.p: **Zero value.** A variable declared without a value starts with its type's zero value: `0`, `""`, `false`, `nil`, or a struct with all fields zeroed.

head: Form
Effect
rows: Declares and infers the type from the value (here, `int`)
Declares with the type's zero value
Without a type, `let` with a number infers `num`, so it can hold decimals later

blocks.note: Variables are scoped to the whole function, not just the block. Don't declare the same name with different types in the same function.

blocks.p: `+` also concatenates strings. There is no `~`: to flip the bits, use `x ^ -1`.
**Conversions** are written as calls: `int(x)`, `num(x)`, `str(x)`, `uint8(x)`, `float32(x)`, `byte(x)`, `rune(x)` and so on.
**if** accepts a statement before the condition, separated by `;`. There are no parentheses around the condition.
**Loops.** There are four forms of `for`, plus `while`:

head: Form
Example
rows: `for i, v := range list { }` and `for k, v := range m { }`

blocks.p: `break` and `continue` accept a label to exit or continue an outer loop.
**switch** compares against each `case`, which can list several values. Cases don't fall through to the next one unless they end with `fallthrough`.
Functions are declared with `fn` at the top level of the file. Every parameter has a type. The result type comes after `->` and, if omitted, is inferred from the `return`.
A function can return multiple values, `-> (int, error)`, and results can be named: a bare `return` returns their current values.
Inside another function, create functions as values with `fn(...) { }`. They capture outer variables (closures).

blocks.note: Declared functions don't accept a variable number of arguments. `...` spreads a list into a call, as in `append(a, b...)`.

blocks.p: **Structs** group typed fields. A literal can give values in order, `Point{1, 2}`, or by name, `Point{y: 2}`. Fields left out get their zero value.
**Methods** are functions with a receiver: `fn (p: Point) dist()` receives a copy, and `fn (p: *Point) move()` receives the original and can modify it.
**Embedding** one struct in another gives the outer struct the inner one's fields and methods.

**Interfaces** are satisfied implicitly: a type satisfies an interface if it has its methods. An interface can embed another. `x.(T)` recovers the stored type and, with `v, ok := x.(T)`, does not panic.
Errors are values of type `error`. Create one with `errors.New("message")` or with any type that has an `Error() -> str` method. Functions that can fail return the error as their last result.

`defer` schedules a call for when the function returns; deferred calls run from last to first. `panic` stops execution and unwinds the calls; `recover`, inside a `defer`, stops the panic. Runtime errors, such as an index out of range, also panic.

head: Function
Use
rows: Prints the values separated by spaces, followed by a newline
Length and capacity of strings, arrays, slices and maps
Appends values to a slice and returns the slice
Copies elements and returns how many were copied
Removes a key from a map
Allocates a zero value and returns a pointer
Stops execution, and recovers inside a defer
Creates an error with the message

blocks.p: Each file is a module. Only names declared with `export` can be used by other files.

head: Import
Effect
rows: Brings names in for direct use
Another file in the project, relative to the current one
Third-party package, installed with `caju pkg add`

blocks.p: Caju comes with a package manager, `caju pkg`. There is no central server: a package is a GitHub repository with a `caju.toml` file at its root. The package name is the repository path, and that is the name programs import.
**Versions.** A published version is a git tag in the `vX.Y.Z` format, matching the `version` in `caju.toml`. If the two don't match, the package manager rejects the package.

**Version selection.** Each dependency states the *minimum* version it needs. When two packages ask for different versions of the same package, the highest of the minimums wins. So the result only changes when a `caju.toml` asks for a higher version, never because someone published a new one. Versions with different MAJOR numbers, such as 1.x and 2.x, are not compatible.

**Compiler version.** The `caju` field of `caju.toml` says which versions of the language the package works with: `"0.6.0"` or `">=0.6.0"` for a minimum, `">=0.5.0, <0.7.0"` for a range, `^` and `~` for compatible versions. `caju pkg` and `caju build` check it for the project and every dependency, and say which version is needed instead of failing halfway through the build.

**Version locking.** `caju.lock` records, for every package used directly or indirectly, the version, the commit and a SHA-256 hash of its files. Commit it, so everyone compiles exactly the same files.

**Verification.** Before compiling, `caju build` and `caju run` check that `caju.lock` is up to date with `caju.toml` and that each package's files match the locked hash. Any mismatch stops the build:

head: Command
What it does
rows: Adds a dependency (default: the latest published version)
Updates dependencies to the latest published version
Downloads what's missing and verifies everything against `caju.lock`
Checks cached packages against the hashes in the lock file
The packages downloaded on this machine, shared by every project and checked against their hash on every reuse
Computes the hash of a package directory

blocks.p: **Where they live.** Packages are downloaded with `git` (the version tag) into the cache at `~/.caju/pkg`. `add`, `remove` and `update` edit only the `[dependencies]` section of `caju.toml`, leaving the rest of the file untouched.

blocks.note: Within a package, files import each other by full path, as in `import "github.com/acme/strutil/extra"`, and a package should only import what is in its own `[dependencies]`.

blocks.p: `extern` declares a function from a Windows DLL, using the `stdcall` (default) or `cdecl` calling convention. Parameters use interface types: `i32`, `u32`, `i64`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64`, `ptr`, `bool`, `str` and `wstr`, and the result can be `void`. These calls are only available in programs compiled with `--target windows`.

head: Command
What it does
rows: Builds a WebAssembly module (runs in Node or in the browser)

list: Goroutines, channels and `select` in the native compiler. The keywords `go`, `chan` and `select` are already reserved.
Maps with struct, array or `any` keys.

playground.title: Playground
playground.lead: Write Caju and run it right here. The compiler itself runs in your browser, compiled to WebAssembly: nothing is sent to a server.
playground.empty: Press Run (or Ctrl+Enter) to see what the program prints.
playground.stats: compiled in {compile} ms · ran in {run} ms
playground.loadFailed: The compiler could not be loaded
playground.badName: Use letters, digits, _ - . and / in the name, and a name that is not in use yet.
playground.how: The Caju compiler is written in Caju and compiles to WebAssembly with `--target wasm`, so it can compile itself to `caju.wasm`. The page downloads that file from the language's latest release, with the standard library. When you press Run, it compiles your program to another WebAssembly module and runs it in a worker, with the output streamed back here. A program can have several files: `main.caju` runs first and imports the others with `import "util"`.

arch.title: How Caju works
arch.lead: From a .caju file to a running program: the stages of the compiler, how values live in memory, the garbage collector, calls and panics, and how the compiler ends up running in your browser. Everything shown here comes from the real compiler.
arch.pipelineLead: The compiler is a chain of stages, each one written in Caju (compiler/*.caju). Follow a small program through them: pick a stage to see what it produces.

stages.name: Source
stages.desc: The program as you wrote it: one or more `.caju` files. The project loader reads the entry file and every file it imports (`import "util"`, `import "std/strings"`, packages from `caju.lock`).

stages.name: Lexer
stages.desc: `lexer.caju` cuts the text into tokens: keywords, names, operators, numbers, texts. Each token keeps its line and column, which is how every error later points at the right place. Line breaks become `NEWLINE` tokens: they end statements.

stages.name: Parser
stages.desc: `parser.caju` is a recursive descent parser: it turns the tokens into a tree of nodes (`Func`, `Return`, `Binary`, `Call`...). A syntax error stops here, with the token it did not expect.

stages.name: Linker
stages.desc: `linker.caju` joins the files into one program: each file becomes a module, only names declared with `export` are visible outside it, and every imported name is resolved to its declaration.

stages.name: Type checker
stages.desc: `types.caju` and `check.caju` infer and check the type of every expression and annotate the tree (`ty="int"`): which call is a function, a method, a conversion; which variables a closure captures. A type error stops here.

stages.name: Code generator
stages.desc: The annotated tree goes straight to machine code, without an intermediate representation. `native.caju` generates x86-64 (with register allocation, loop versioning, inlining); `wasm.caju` generates WebAssembly. The runtime (`rt/*.caju`: allocator, collector, maps, panics) is compiled along with the program.

stages.name: Executable
stages.desc: `image.caju` writes an ELF file for Linux or a PE file for Windows: a static executable of about 50 KB, with no libc and no dynamic linking. With `--target wasm`, the result is a WebAssembly module that runs in a browser or in Node.

arch.codegenNote: Both versions of `add` take the arguments from the stack. The x86-64 code moves them to registers (`rsi`, `rdi`); in WebAssembly they stay in the linear memory, where the garbage collector can see them.
arch.bootstrapLead: The Caju compiler is written in Caju. To get the first one, a small compiler written in JavaScript is used once; after that, the compiler compiles its own source.

bootstrap.title: Stage 0
bootstrap.desc: `bootstrap/*.js`: the original compiler, in JavaScript, run by Node.

bootstrap.title: Stage 1
bootstrap.desc: Stage 0 compiles `compiler/main.caju`: a native `caju`, made by the JavaScript compiler.

bootstrap.title: Stage 2
bootstrap.desc: Stage 1 compiles the same source: now a compiler made by a Caju compiler.

bootstrap.title: Stage 3
bootstrap.desc: Stage 2 compiles it again. Stage 2 and stage 3 must be **identical byte for byte**: the compiler reproduces itself.

bootstrap.title: caju.wasm
bootstrap.desc: With `--target wasm`, the compiler compiles itself to WebAssembly; `caju.wasm` then compiles itself to the same bytes too.

arch.bootstrapNote: Every change to the compiler is checked this way, besides the test suite: if stage 2 and stage 3 differ, something in the compiler changed the meaning of the compiler itself.
arch.valuesLead: Every value fits in one 64-bit word. Numbers and booleans are the word itself; everything else is a pointer to an object made by the runtime.

values.title: Text
values.desc: A pointer to `[length][UTF-8 bytes][0]`. Texts never change: `+` makes a new one, and the same literal is shared by the whole program.

values.title: List
values.desc: A pointer to a header `[data, length, capacity]`. Slicing makes a new header over the same data; `append` writes into the free capacity or copies to a bigger array.

values.title: Struct
values.desc: A pointer to an object with one word per field. Assigning a struct copies it (as in Go); a `*Point` is the same pointer without the copy.

values.title: Map
values.desc: The entries in insertion order, plus an index of 32-bit slots (a tag from the hash and a position), at most 3/4 full. `range` walks the entries in order.

values.title: any
values.desc: A pointer to a box `[descriptor, value]`. The type descriptor says what the value is: the runtime uses it for `x.(T)`, type switches, `==`, printing and method calls through interfaces.

arch.gcLead: The runtime allocates objects in 64 KB pages and collects them with mark and sweep, written in Caju (rt/gc.caju). Try it: the roots are the program's stack and globals.

gcSteps.idle: Each object is reachable from a root or not. Press Mark.
gcSteps.marking: Marking: from the roots, every object reached is marked, then the objects they point to.
gcSteps.marked: Everything reachable is marked. The rest is garbage: press Sweep.
gcSteps.swept: Swept: the unmarked objects are free memory again. The program goes on with the live ones.

arch.gcNote: The collector is **conservative**: any word on the stack or in an object that looks like a pointer into an object keeps it alive. That is why a pointer must never live only in a register during a call, and why the WebAssembly version keeps every value that must survive a call on a stack in memory. A collection starts when the memory allocated since the last one passes what survived it (at least 8 MB).
arch.callsLead: Every call pushes its arguments on the stack and every function keeps its locals in a frame. defer, panic and recover are part of the runtime.

calls.title: A call
calls.desc: The caller pushes the arguments (and the closure, for a function value) and calls; the callee finds argument i of n at a fixed offset and makes room for its locals. Results 2, 3... travel in `g.ret`.

calls.title: The depth limit
calls.desc: A counter of calls left starts at 10,000 and each call takes one: the 10,001st nested call stops with "Too much recursion" instead of crashing.

calls.title: defer
calls.desc: A function with `defer` links a record into a list (`rt_dtop`); each `defer` adds a node with the function and its already evaluated arguments. They run from last to first when the function returns.

calls.title: panic and recover
calls.desc: `panic` runs the deferred calls from the newest record to the oldest. If one of them calls `recover()`, execution jumps back to the function that deferred it, which returns normally. In WebAssembly that jump is a wasm exception.

arch.browserLead: The playground runs the real compiler, compiled to WebAssembly, without a server.

browser.title: The release
browser.desc: Each GitHub release has `caju-wasm.tar.gz`: the compiler as `caju.wasm`, the standard library and the runtime as text, and a small JavaScript host.

browser.title: The worker
browser.desc: The page starts a Web Worker that loads `caju.wasm` and an in-memory file system with the library.

browser.title: Compile
browser.desc: Your files go into that file system and `caju build --target wasm` runs inside `caju.wasm`, as it would on Linux: the host answers its system calls (open, read, write...).

browser.title: Run
browser.desc: The new module runs in the same worker; what it writes comes back to the page as it is written. Stop terminates the worker.

tools.title: caju test
tools.desc: Finds `*_test.caju` files and runs them: `describe`, `it` and `expect` from `std/testing`.

tools.title: caju pkg
tools.desc: Packages are GitHub repositories; minimal version selection and a `caju.lock` with SHA-256 hashes.

tools.title: caju mcp
tools.desc: A Model Context Protocol server: AI assistants check, run and test Caju code with structured results.

ai.title: Caju for AI assistants
ai.lead: caju mcp is a Model Context Protocol server built into the caju command. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor and other assistants use the compiler through tools with structured results: they read the language reference, look up the standard library, and check, run and test code.
ai.setupLead: It comes with the caju command: there is nothing else to install.
ai.otherClients: Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code and other clients
ai.setupNote: Use the full path of `caju` (`~/.local/bin/caju` with the installer) if the client does not see your `PATH`. The server reads JSON-RPC messages on its standard input, one per line.
ai.toolsLead: Checking, running and testing answer with JSON, so the assistant never parses the compiler's text output. The code graph tools answer with one short line per symbol, instead of whole files: the graph lives in the server's memory and answers in about 2 ms.

tools.name: caju_check
tools.desc: Type-checks without generating code. Every error comes with its file, line, column and stage (syntax, type, link...).

tools.name: caju_run
tools.desc: Compiles and runs with a time limit. If the program does not compile, the answer is the diagnostics; otherwise the exit code and the output.

tools.name: caju_test
tools.desc: Runs `*_test.caju` files, optionally only the tests whose name has a given text, and returns the counts and the report.

tools.name: caju_docs
tools.desc: Searches the exported functions, methods, structs and constants of the standard library, with their doc comments.

tools.name: caju_reference
tools.desc: The language reference, whole or only the sections about a topic. Also available as the resource `caju://reference`.

tools.name: caju_find
tools.desc: Searches the symbols of a project by name, the closest first: one line per symbol, with its signature and file:lines.

tools.name: caju_symbol
tools.desc: One symbol: signature, doc comment, fields and methods, who calls it, what it calls and what uses it. With `code`, its source lines.

tools.name: caju_related
tools.desc: Callers, callees, implementations, uses, fields or methods of a symbol, up to 5 levels deep.

tools.name: caju_call_path
tools.desc: The shortest chain of calls from one function to another, through interface methods too.

tools.name: caju_outline
tools.desc: Everything a file declares, with fields and methods, without the bodies.

tools.name: caju_pkg
tools.desc: Adds, removes, installs and verifies packages. Downloads go to a cache shared by every project and are reused only if their SHA-256 hash still matches.

ai.demoLead: An assistant (Claude Sonnet 5.5) converting a Go-style program to Caju with the MCP tools. It is one of the runs of the comparison below, shortened, in its original English.
ai.benchLead: The same three tasks, done by Claude Code with only the `caju` command in a shell, or with only the MCP tools. Same model, same prompt, an empty directory with the task's files; each result checked afterwards.

benchTasks.title: Write a program
benchTasks.desc: The 5 most frequent words of a text, sorted by count and then alphabetically.

benchTasks.title: Go to Caju
benchTasks.desc: A program written in Go style must become valid Caju and print two given lines.

benchTasks.title: Write tests
benchTasks.desc: At least 4 tests for a stack module that has a hidden bug.

findings.title: It reads before it writes
findings.desc: With MCP, every run began with `caju_reference` and `caju_docs`, then wrote the program once. Most programs were right the first time.

findings.title: Without it, the compiler is the manual
findings.desc: With the CLI, the assistant learned Caju from error messages: `caju --help`, then small probe programs, one construct at a time, rewriting after each error. One run hit the 40-turn limit still probing the syntax.

findings.title: Errors point at the fix
findings.desc: A diagnostic with line, column and stage takes the assistant straight to the line to change, instead of reading and guessing from text.

findings.title: It went looking for the server
findings.desc: In a first round where `caju mcp` was not blocked, CLI runs found it in `caju --help` and spoke JSON-RPC to it from the shell to read the reference.

ai.benchNote: Two runs per task and mode, one model and small tasks: the direction is clear, the exact ratios are not. The CLI runs could not use other shell commands. Programs, logs summary and method in `bench/mcp` of the language repository.
ai.whyTitle: Why a new language needs this
ai.why: An assistant has never seen Caju while it learned, and Caju looks enough like Go to be written as Go. The server gives it the real reference, the real names of the library and exact positions for every error, so it stops guessing.
